articles.title: Carson Hocevar’s Private Text Messages Surface in Joe Gibbs Racing Lawsuit
articles.summary: Carson Hocevar’s private text messages are now part of the ongoing legal battle involving Joe Gibbs Racing, Chris Gabehart and Spire Motorsports.And in typic...
articles.body:
Carson Hocevar's private text messages are now part of the ongoing legal battle involving Joe Gibbs Racing, Chris Gabehart and Spire Motorsports.

And in typical Hocevar fashion, there's some humor involved.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, FOX Sports' Bob Pockrass shared text exchanges included in court filings that revealed conversations between Hocevar and Spire Motorsports co-owner Jeff Dickerson, as well as a separate exchange between Hocevar and Gabehart.

At the center of both conversations? Hocevar's struggles at Martinsville Speedway.

The 23-year-old NASCAR Cup Series driver apparently was eager to tap into Gabehart's expertise, and he wasn't particularly shy about acknowledging how much help he needed.

Carson Hocevar Gets Brutally Honest Response From Spire Motorsports Boss

In a text exchange dated Feb. 5, shortly after NASCAR's preseason Clash, Hocevar approached Dickerson about the possibility of getting some assistance from Gabehart.

"Do you think Gabehart can help me for Martinsville?" Hocevar asked.

Dickerson's response was rather unforgiving.

"No one can help THAT much," he replied before adding, "But he can maybe get you closer."

Hocevar, never one to shy away from a little self-deprecating humor, fired back with a reference to late NASCAR driver Dick Trickle and a suggestion that he'd rather spend the weekend dirt late model racing.

"Okay then we are throwing Dick Trickle in the car and going DLM racing that weekend instead," Hocevar wrote.

Eleven days later, the subject of Martinsville came up again, this time in a conversation directly with Gabehart.

Carson Hocevar's Text Messages With Chris Gabehart Revealed

On Feb. 16, Gabehart reached out to Hocevar following a discussion earlier that day, expressing his excitement about working together and encouraging the young driver to contact him whenever he needed anything.

Hocevar welcomed Gabehart and wasted little time bringing up his least favorite subject.

"aka how do I get around martinsville lol," Hocevar wrote as part of his response.

Gabehart expressed confidence that he could help Hocevar with more than just Martinsville, prompting another candid admission from the driver.

"Perfect. I am just trying to find the lead lap," Hocevar replied.

The exchanges offer a rare glimpse into Hocevar's conversations away from the cameras, including his willingness to acknowledge his shortcomings and seek advice from one of NASCAR's experienced competition figures.

Pockrass noted that he was unsure how much relevance the exchanges had to the issue of JGR information sharing. The messages he published do not themselves show Gabehart providing proprietary JGR information.

For all the serious allegations surrounding the ongoing lawsuit, the newly public conversations also revealed something considerably more lighthearted: Hocevar's frustration with getting around NASCAR's famous half-mile short track, and a team owner who wasn't about to let him off easy.

articles.title: Max Verstappen showed 'race craft' edge over George Russell and Kimi Antonelli during Las Vegas GP, says Jacques Villeneuve
articles.summary: Max Verstappen withstood pressure from Mercedes' George Russell and Kimi Antonelli on his way to winning a thrilling Las Vegas GP for Red Bull; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live on Sky Sports this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
articles.body:
Verstappen retained the lead from pole position at the start but was challenged by Russell and then later Antonelli for almost the entire 50-lap race amid near constant changes of position throughout the field, but the Red Bull driver expertly saw off their best efforts before both made late errors to drop down the order.

Antonelli has already been crowned 2026 world champion after Mercedes' dominance early in the season helped him build a significant advantage, but Verstappen is putting together an ominous finish to the year, with the four-time world champion having won four of the last six races and claimed nine successive podiums.

Sky Sports F1 pundit and 1997 F1 world champion Villeneuve said after the race: "It was exciting. People will say there was a battery involved [in all the passes], but it doesn't matter.

"We saw some race craft. Max was above and the two Mercedes drivers were lacking in that respect.

"And what it is telling us is that unless next year Mercedes have a car that's superior, they can't win because there's something missing."

A combination of factors, most notably the extreme power of the slipstream effect, meant there were more than 350 overtakes during a breathless race at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit.

The lead changed hands 34 times, but every time Verstappen was overtaken, which on almost every occasion was by a Mercedes, the four-time world champion retook his position within a few corners.

Russell locked up and hit a barrier as he tried to pass Antonelli for second in the closing stages, before the Italian suffered a loss of power at the start of the final lap after incorrectly lifting off the throttle as he was preparing to mount a final challenge to Verstappen.

Villeneuve was also impressed by the drives of seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton and last year's title winner Lando Norris, who took advantage of the Mercedes errors to finish second ahead of his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri.

Hamilton could have also ended up on the podium had it not been for him spinning in a contentious collision with his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.

"You could see that Lewis had good race craft as well as Lando," Villeneuve added.

"It was really fun to see. We saw today a race where you don't need pit stops, you don't need tyres that degrade.

"We had a race where drivers could push like qualifying laps all the time and that allowed them to race. It was great fun."

articles.title: Alonso, un aliado para Loeb en el Dakar: "Intentaré ayudarle a ganarlo"
articles.standfirst: El asturiano considera a su nuevo compañero en el Dakar "el mejor piloto de rallies de la historia"
articles.summary: El asturiano considera a su nuevo compañero en el Dakar "el mejor piloto de rallies de la historia"
articles.body: Esta ha sido la semana en la que Fernando Alonso ha confirmado su presencia en el Dakar 2027, y eso ha vuelto a poner en el foco a la carrera -este año- africana... y a muchas de las historias que le rodean. Una de ellas es la búsqueda de otro de los grandes de la historia del automovilismo, Sebastien Loeb, de su primer triunfo en el rally más duro del planeta. Una lucha que, de momento, le ha costado ya una década (la de 2027 será su undécima participación, en las que ha acumulado tres segundos puestos y cinco presencias en el podio. Nadie duda de que Loeb vale uno o varios Dakar, pero el caso es que hasta ahora no lo ha conseguido. Y su próxima intentona será con Aston Martin y al lado de un bicampeón del mundo de Fórmula 1. Lógicamente, la prensa francesa ha puesto el foco en el hecho de que Fernando Alonso vaya a ser compañero de equipo de su estrella. Así, Canal + Francia preguntó al español por esa circunstancia. "Es un privilegio. Para mi es el mejor piloto de rallies de la historia, por los títulos, la forma en la que pilota, en la que ataca siempre, su consistencia...", explicaba el español, que aprovechará también esa circunstancia para "Hay muchas cosas que aprender de él, nunca hemos corrido juntos [en el Dakar 2020 Loeb no fue de la partida]. Así que estoy deseando hacerlo", añadía. Alonso, que disputará su segundo Dakar con el objetivo de seguir adquiriendo experiencia en una disciplina aún nueva para él, se ofreció a poder apoyar a Loeb en la búsqueda del triunfo que ha guiado su carrera durante la última década: "Mis objetivos en el Dakar no son los mismos que los suyos, obviamente. Si puedo prestarle algún apoyo, intentaré ayudarle a ganarlo", aseguró.

articles.title: Alonso y la paternidad: "Muchas noches me he preguntado si me estoy perdiendo momentos importantes"
articles.standfirst: El asturiano se sincera ante Aston Martin tras un curso positivo en lo personal, difícil en lo deportivo y ante un 2027 movido
articles.summary: El asturiano se sincera ante Aston Martin tras un curso positivo en lo personal, difícil en lo deportivo y ante un 2027 movido
articles.body: Fernando Alonso cerrará la temporada 2026 al borde de los 450 Grandes Premios disputados que cumplirá en el amanecer del curso 2027, en la segunda cita de Arabia Saudí. Será también su temporada 24 en la Fórmula 1 tras tomar la decisión de seguir después de un 2026 decepcionante. A los 45 años, su ambición no ha cambiado y sigue buscando hacer historia, con la participación en el Rally Dakar que arrancará en Portugal, se desarrollará en Marruecos y en el que volverá con la mecánica campeona de la última edición. Nadie descubrirá a estas alturas de la película a Alonso, su actitud y lo que fundamenta su decisión de seguir detrás del volante. Tiene el talento y el convencimiento propio de ser superior a sus rivales. Aunque lo más complejo es tener un equipo a la altura que garantice oportunidades, más si cabe en una Fórmula 1 con brecha entre los cuatro equipos de cabeza y el resto. Pero no todo es sencillo. La posibilidad de un paso al frente se pone en duda y se suman unas circunstancias personales del piloto que hacían de su decisión de seguir una de las más complejas de su carrera deportiva. No fue como la primera retirada por aburrimiento con lo que ocurría en la F1 y el sueño de ganar en otros lugares. Alonso ya es todo, y gana un peso gigante factores clave, como su reciente paternidad. No era el asunto más tratado por el piloto, como es lógico. Pero en el Undercut de Aston Martin sí desveló lo que le ha generado como piloto el ser padre de un bebé. "Ha sido lo más difícil [compaginar la familia y las carreras]. Muchas noches, a lo largo del año, me he preguntado si me estaré perdiendo momentos importantes", confesó en la web del equipo británico. "Antes de ser padre, no entendía del todo lo que significa tener hijos y lo difícil que es estar lejos tan a menudo. Ahora lo comprendo perfectamente", agregó. Pero hay una parte que le da motivación para seguir. "También pienso en mi equipo. Mi mecánico principal tuvo un hijo con su pareja hace tres años y pronto tendrán otro. Pienso en la gente del equipo porque trabaja más duro que yo. Pasan más horas en el circuito que yo. Viajan antes que yo y regresan después. Pero trabajan con gran esfuerzo y siguen motivados", reflexionó. Le da fuerzas. "Ver eso me ayuda a entender la posición privilegiada que ocupa y me impulsa a esforzarme más", lanzó. Y en esa motivación hay un punto más con seguir construyendo legado más allá de la F1. El Dakar es seguro, y no descarta el regreso a las 500 Millas de Indianápolis y las 24 Horas de Le Mans con la Triple Corona entre ceja y ceja. "Me plantearía volver a la Indy porque la relación entre riesgo y recompensa es mayor que cualquier otra. Hay riesgo, requeriría preparación, pero la recompensa es un logro histórico", comentó. "También me planteo volver a las 24 Horas de Le Mans. Pero, por el momento, no tengo planes más allá del Dakar y sólo me interesaría algo muy emblemático y prestigioso", cerró.

articles.title: Ducati ajusta cuentas: "Ha quedado aún más claro el motivo de fichar a Márquez"
articles.standfirst: Fue el fichaje que reventó MotoGP en 2024, recibió críticas y su CEO del departamento de carreras, Gigi Dall'Igna, tiene claro el mensaje
articles.summary: Fue el fichaje que reventó MotoGP en 2024, recibió críticas y su CEO del departamento de carreras, Gigi Dall'Igna, tiene claro el mensaje
articles.body: No existe una resaca más dulce que la de Ducati y su estrellón, Marc Márquez, tras el décimo título mundial de motociclismo del prodigio de Cervera. Tras cruzar la meta de Portimao se desató la locura en la grava, alcanzó al box y durante cada segundo de la celebración. También sigue al volver a España, acordarse de los que merecen la pena y dejar atrás los que no aportan (como el propio 93 señaló). Y llegará a la fiesta final del Gran Premio de la Comunitat Valenciana para un baño de masas final antes del reto de la nueva era con las 850cc. En esa celebración también hay espacio a reivindicaciones. Algunas van dentro de la propia épica del Mundial, que cambió con aquella afrenta a Ducati en Mugello ante el show de Aprilia. Otras a las decisiones que han cambiado MotoGP como tal y son vitales para entender los dos títulos del 93 con su moto roja. El primero es su propio fichaje en 2024, cuando sólo llevaba un puñado de carreras en la moto del Gresini (sin la evolución de las oficiales) e impuso su candidatura a un Jorge Martín que iba líder y acabó ganando aquel título para marcharse con el 1 a Aprilia. Márquez quería ser oficial y no dudó en señalar que sus opciones eran pocas. El resto... es historia. Ese fichaje nació del impulso del gurú técnico del equipo y CEO del departamento de carreras, Gigi Dall'Igna. "Prevalece nuestra decisión de ficharle y su inquebrantable determinación de unirse a Ducati. El motivo ha quedado aún más claro", relata el italiano en su Linkedin. Era de los más emocionados cuando hablaba con Márquez en Portimao y valora al ilerdense como alguien único. "Un fenómeno renacido que sabe dejar huella sin ser el más rápido en pista. Mentalmente, técnicamente y estratégicamente, roza la perfección: ha evolucionado y ha alcanzado un nivel ejemplar de madurez. Sabe qué hacer y cuándo, aprovecha, optimiza y saca lo mejor de todo. Tiene siempre una marcha extra", define el italiano. Nunca ha dudado en colocarle como el mejor de la historia, y eso que ha trabajado con todos los grandes modernos, como Valentino Rossi, Casey Stoner o Jorge Lorenzo. Y nada del título en pista es tan especial como la remontada. Con las lágrimas del box en Le Mans de Marc, la ovación al acabar en Mugello o el cambio de marcha en una temporada brutal. Siendo Aprilia la moto más completa, consiguiendo limitarla y sabiendo jugar en el tablero que Rivola o los pilotos de los de Noale imponían. "Este título pone de relieve puntos fuertes más allá de la superioridad técnica. Tuvimos rivales muy fuertes y rápidos que honraron al título con los que nos intercambiamos victorias y récords. Les damos la enhorabuena por subir tanto el listón", cuenta Dall'Igna. Sin ocultar el punto de inflexión de la carrera de casa. "Teníamos una enorme distancia, pero no nos detuvimos y la fe en el título no flaqueó", apunta el italiano. Márquez, por su lado, sí que reconoció que tenía más dudas. Pero que su entorno le impulsó. "Prevaleció la filosofía de empresa: la unidad, forma de ser, trabajar y ganar juntos. También de perder", resalta el jefe del departamento de carreras. Y hasta pide el último impulso. "El compromiso y la concentración se centra en el título de constructores. Está en juego y lucharemos hasta el final", cierra. El de equipos ya es del oficial de Aprilia con Martín y Bezzecchi, y de constructores hay nueve puntos de renta a favor de los de Noale (598 a 589).

articles.title: 'It's a rich man's sport': Jeet Jhabakh opens up on the financial challenges facing Indian motorsport
articles.summary: Hyderabad-based racer Jeet Jhabakh, alongside co-driver Musa Sherif, recently won the 2026 FIA Asia-Pacific Rally Championship (APRC), becoming the first
articles.body: Hyderabad-based racer Jeet Jhabakh, alongside co-driver Musa Sherif, recently won the 2026 FIA Asia-Pacific Rally Championship (APRC), becoming the first driver in the championship's 38-year history to win the overall title in a two-wheel-drive car. The duo also created history as the first all-Indian driver and co-driver pairing to clinch the continental championship.For Jeet, however, the victory is more than a personal milestone. He hopes it will open doors for Indian racers who have the talent but struggle to find the financial backing and international exposure needed to compete at the highest level.Unlike cricket, where a bat and ball can provide the starting point for a young player, motorsport requires access to specialised equipment, vehicles, training and technical support, with the costs increasing significantly as drivers move up the competitive ladder."It is an extremely expensive sport. In cricket, most people just require a bat and a ball to play. But in motorsport, you require a full-fledged car, and as you go higher and higher, the car gets more expensive. It is definitely a rich man's sport," Jeet told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive conversation.From cricket to cars: How Jeet Jhabakh found his callingLike many Indian children, Jeet grew up playing cricket, but his interest gradually shifted towards cars as he began following Formula One and the World Rally Championship (WRC). With his family already involved in the automobile business, the transition into motorsport came naturally."Honestly, just like every other child in India, I also first started with cricket. We all could have fun playing cricket in the streets next to our houses. The first sport you tend to gravitate towards is basically a sport which is very accessible," Jeet said."As I grew older, I started watching a lot of Formula One and WRC. That's when I realised my heart had always been in cars. Fortunately, my family business is also related to cars, so it kind of tied in well with me. When I got an opportunity to get into motorsport, I jumped at it. There was no looking back at all."Despite eventually finding success in rallying, Jeet's childhood motorsport inspiration came from Formula One legend Michael Schumacher. He admired the German's dominance but was equally impressed by his race intelligence, strategy and ability to look beyond outright speed, something he has come to appreciate in his own racing career."Michael Schumacher was the person we used to really follow back in the day. He was absolutely dominant. Even though he might not have been the absolute fastest on track, his strategies and thinking were always on point," Jeet said."I always wondered whether speed was the only reason you win or whether it was a holistic approach. Now I have realised it is the holistic approach. It's not pure speed always. You have to think out of the box and be able to adapt."Jeet's experience in both circuit racing and rallying has also given him an understanding of the different skill sets the two disciplines demand.Unlike circuit racing, where drivers compete against each other on a fixed track, rallying is a race against the clock across a series of timed stages conducted on different surfaces, including gravel, dirt, tarmac and snow. Drivers are guided by their co-drivers, who read out pace notes describing upcoming corners, jumps and road conditions."In racing, you start together and compete with another person. You're fighting for that tenth of a second, pushing really hard. But in rallying, you don't compete with each other at the same point in time. There's a gap between the car in front of you and the car behind you," he explained."You tend to stick to your notes, do your best and hope that your time is better than the others. Both disciplines require different sets of skills, but they tie together in their own way."The expensive reality of motorsport in IndiaIndia has produced several prominent rally drivers over the years, including five-time national rally champion Hari Singh, seven-time national champion Naren Kumar and Gaurav Gill, who in 2013 became the first Indian to win the overall Asia-Pacific Rally Championship title.But for many aspiring Indian racers, securing the financial backing needed to build a career in motorsport remains one of the biggest challenges, something Jeet acknowledges from his own experience.Having never participated in competitive karting, Jeet began his competitive career through a single-make championship. His victories in the series helped him secure a sponsored drive and eventually become a factory driver for Utsavya Motorsports in 2019, an opportunity that allowed him to continue racing without having to carry the entire financial burden himself."After I won it again in 2019, I became the factory driver for Utsavya Motorsports. I was sponsored completely by them. Because of that, I got an opportunity to drive for four and a half years. I was very fortunate. A lot of people, unfortunately, don't get that opportunity," Jeet said.'Indian drivers have the talent': What separates India from Europe?Beyond the cost of competing, Jeet believes one of the biggest differences between Indian drivers and their European counterparts is the amount of time they are able to dedicate to the sport.While drivers in more established motorsport ecosystems have greater opportunities to pursue racing as a full-time professional career, many Indian drivers have to balance their sporting ambitions with regular employment to finance their careers."In India, I cannot make this my only source of income because it gets very difficult. We are all working something or the other. Monday to Friday, we are working hard to make a little bit of money for ourselves to spend on racing and rallying," he explained."Over there, they are able to take this as a professional career. They are driving Monday to Friday and competing on Saturday and Sunday. With that amount of time in the car, training and guidance, there is bound to be a difference in quality over time."His own APRC victory, he feels, is evidence that Indian drivers can compete at the international level if provided with similar opportunities."If we get the same opportunity, I personally feel Indian drivers can get to that level in due course of time. I think we can compete in it. This championship is a testament that it is possible," he said.Can Formula One's return change the fortunes of Indian motorsport?India's stint as a Formula One host between 2011 and 2013 introduced a generation of fans to international circuit racing. However, the departure of the Indian Grand Prix left a gap in the country's motorsport calendar and limited opportunities for fans to experience the sport at the highest level.For Jeet, who grew up watching Formula One and dreaming of being part of its ecosystem, the departure was particularly disappointing."Honestly, it broke my heart as a kid when Formula One decided to pull out of India. Every child who is into cars, the first thing is that you want to be a part of the whole system. When it pulled out, I was just like, man, I wish it continued," he recalled.Jeet believes the return of major international racing events, alongside the growth of domestic competitions such as the Indian Racing Festival, could help attract new fans, encourage corporate investment and create better opportunities for Indian racers."Even small races like the Indian Racing Festival coming back to India is a massive opportunity. You get to see the tracks and fast cars. That's when the public gets to know that something like this can happen," he said."A lot of media today covers sports like cricket. Badminton is also getting a lot more attention, but motorsport, even our national championships, are not really covered in the media. When something like Formula One or WRC comes to India and there is a lot of media presence, people will start getting involved. When people start watching it, more money flows into it through advertisements and sponsorships."For now, Jeet hopes his APRC triumph will encourage more businesses to invest in Indian motorsport and provide upcoming drivers with the kind of opportunities he was fortunate enough to receive early in his career."I'm hoping that this championship we've won will open doors for a lot of sponsorship, not just for myself, but for a lot of people in the country as well. There is a lot of talent here in India. Why don't we set up something in India for upcoming drivers?" he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.standfirst: La guerra en Ferrari está más que viva, tiene personalidades enfrentadas y puntos de vista completamente diferentes que hace difícil pensar en un entendimiento
articles.summary: La guerra en Ferrari está más que viva, tiene personalidades enfrentadas y puntos de vista completamente diferentes que hace difícil pensar en un entendimiento
articles.body: No se soportan". No es una frase atribuida a algún protagonista principal, pero es el mensaje que la siempre relevante prensa italiana, en este caso la revista AutoRacer, traslada sobre la guerra que en la Scuderia Ferrari se vive entre Lewis Hamilton y Charles Leclerc y alcanzó dimensiones bíblicas tras el toque del monegasco al británico en Las Vegas. La tensión escaló y el choque entre dos estrellas de la Fórmula 1 será uno de los asuntos principales para las dos rondas que faltan para la conclusión del curso 2026. La polémica Hamilton - Leclerc no es un asunto menor. Viene de dos pilotos con talento de campeón del mundo, su sueldo no está lejos de los 100 millones entre los dos y compiten para un equipo que es más que una simple estructura. Ferrari es una religión y una forma de ser. Y si los pilotos están en guerra, nadie es capaz de solucionarlo y tampoco llegan las victorias... Se forman los problemas. La suya es una guerra es más que lo que ocurre en pista, las peticiones de Hamilton que Leclerc no escucha... y ni siquiera el toque de Las Vegas. Parece, en primer lugar, un asunto de estado que articula lo que Ferrari quiere ser. Por ello llegó Hamilton como una petición de John Elkann, su presidente. También tiene a Fred Vasseur en el cargo de jefe de equipo, una pieza fundamental en la carrera del siete veces campeón. Y se le ha permitido pasar un 2025 de dudas para liderar al 2026 con claves técnicas y un pilotaje de los coches nuevos que recuerda a la mejor versión del británico. "Mi ADN", repitió el 44. Pero, en paralelo, Leclerc sigue siendo el Predestinato. El hombre llamado a romper la sequía de Ferrari. El favorito de aficionados y de muchos en Maranello. También de los que no pueden ver a Hamilton a su lado, pues el británico es más especial en el trato como su equipo y añoran a un Sainz que optaba por construir equipo y no señalar. Y la tensión en pista no ha ayudado. "Han hecho la paz", recalcaba Vigna, CEO de Ferrari. La última duró dos carreras. Porque es Fórmula 1 y dos pilotos con talento élite colisionan. También con personalidad. Por supuesto, afecta en un campeonato que siempre tiene revisiones según pasa el tiempo. "Podríamos haber ganado a Antonelli", decía Hamilton sobre esas dudas en el equipo que lastraron su curso. También faltó elegir al piloto de cada momento, con el británico lanzado tras ganar en Montmeló y un Leclerc capaz de ir al alza durante el verano. En el cara a cara, eso sí, hay igualdad y lógica para no colocar a una ficha en mejor lugar. Leclerc gana en clasificaciones (12-9), pero cae, por la mínima, en puntos totales (267-250), carreras (11-10) y abandonos (1-3) con el 44. Además, hay voces importantes, como desde la BBC, que hasta recalcan que hay contratos que entran en conflicto. Desde Gran Bretaña explican que Leclerc tiene firmado ser el primer piloto de su equipo y que a Hamilton le habría dado teóricamente igual... Pero en pista la tensión sigue y la intervención de Vasseur tras el problema de Las Vegas resumió que no hay nada arreglado ni seguro dentro del equipo. "Es inaceptable", cerró el galo. Están en el foco, sí o sí, para los dos Grandes Premios que restan del 2026.

articles.title: Aston Martin vuelve a bajar a Alonso para el inicio de un Gran Premio
articles.standfirst: El asturiano no participará en la primera sesión de entrenamientos libres en Qatar y Jak Crawford toma su asiento
articles.summary: El asturiano no participará en la primera sesión de entrenamientos libres en Qatar y Jak Crawford toma su asiento
articles.body: S e repite la historia: Fernando Alonso no estará presente en el inicio de un Gran Premio. No lo hizo en el último disputado, en Las Vegas, aunque tampoco afectó porque el fin de semana en Nevada vino marcado por un día de libres pasado por agua. Y tampoco lo hará en Qatar, con la decisión de Aston Martin de brindar una nueva oportunidad a Jak Crawford, piloto reserva de la estructura, en la primera sesión de entrenamientos libres. Crawford era el elegido para salir en el Libre 1 de Las Vegas, pero el diluvio en el Strip le dejó sin participar más allá de una problemática vuelta de instalación. Ante ese problema, Aston repite estrategia y bajará a Alonso en el inicio de un fin de semana. Aunque el de Qatar es bastante diferente al de la carrera anterior, con demasiada influencia de la unidad de potencia Honda. En Losail la cosa debería ser diferente. Pasará de perder esos 2,5 o tres segundos por recta de Las Vegas a un circuito en el que puede defenderse. Eso sí, la curva rápida que domina en Qatar parece ser otro reto par un motor que claramente es el menos competitivo de la parrilla de la clase reina. Con la duda sobre si tendrán que montar una unidad nueva, algo que daba por hecho el asturiano. "Sí, está rota", comentó tras abandonar en Las Vegas. Aunque quizá Losail genere oportunidades. Es una carrera con límite de vueltas por neumático, el calor es el elemento dominante y Alonso suele rendir. Allí logró su primer podio -2021- en su regreso a la F1 con Alpine y encontró el mejor rendimiento del curso pasado, con un cuarto puesto en la clasificación sprint. En carrera, fue séptimo tanto en la corta como en la de domingo. Un resultado que en 2026 equivaldría al mejor del curso, pues el límite sigue en el octavo que ocupó en Malasia. Además, el 9º de Holanda y 10º de Mónaco son sus únicas presencias en zona de puntos. En clave Crawford, el americano competirá en su séptimo Gran Premio como piloto de desarrollo. En su currículum destaca el subcampeonato de la última campaña de la F2 y sigue sumando kilómetros con un coche de la primera categoría por el que apuesta e invierte para encontrar un hueco en una parrilla de 2027 que tiene a todos sus pilotos cerrados a excepción de Bearman y Haas.

articles.title: What next for Ferrari after Charles Leclerc, Lewis Hamilton's latest collision with No 1 driver and consequences up for debate
articles.summary: Listen to the latest edition of The F1 Show podcast as Simon Lazenby, David Croft and Jamie Chadwick debate what's next at Ferrari after another driver clash; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
articles.body:
Just two races after a fierce battle when running first and second on the opening lap in Mexico City cost the team victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen and led to clear-the-air discussions, the team-mates collided when battling over sixth place in Las Vegas in an incident Leclerc was found at fault for by the stewards and then received the post-race ire of team boss Frederic Vasseur.

Vasseur has said such incidents "cannot continue" but how does the Frenchman get on top of the situation heading towards 2027, when the team will be hoping to launch a fresh bid to end what stands as an 18-year world title drought?

The Ferrari fallout proved a central topic on the latest edition of Sky Sports' The F1 Show podcast ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, in which host Simon Lazenby was joined by David Croft and Jamie Chadwick.

Asked how big the problems between Hamilton and Leclerc were becoming for Ferrari, Chadwick said: "Significant when you think about what they're going to potentially be going into next year with.

"I think this is the time of the year where you don't want to be having these kinds of conflicts because suddenly it will escalate and it will mean that more serious conversation is going to be had in the background."

Speaking on Sky Sports F1 after Sunday's incident in Las Vegas, Jacques Villeneuve, the 1997 title winner, suggested Leclerc - who is in his eighth season with the Scuderia - had "lost" the leadership of the team to Hamilton, who is in his second, and "if there's one of the two drivers knows how to win championships, it's Lewis".

Villeneuve did, however, question whether Ferrari would be able to prioritise Hamilton contractually.

Hamilton said after the race that he has "never asked" for No 1 status at the team, although implied they could have given him more backing when he was second to Kimi Antonelli and around 40 points ahead of Leclerc in the championship earlier this season.

And although Hamilton and Leclerc are both among the sport's biggest names and most-talented drivers, Croft believes events of this season have effectively forced the team's hand and they need to prioritise one over the other in order to achieve better results.

"Whether Lewis Hamilton is asking to be No 1 or not, I don't think matters any more," said Croft.

"I think the way things have panned out this season the matter has been forced.

"Lewis has to be the No 1 because Charles keeps putting himself in a position whereby Ferrari suffer when the two drivers come together.

"He got the penalty on Sunday. Whether you think it's a penalty or not, the move was ambitious and it was ambitious if it was a move on Lando Norris, it was ambitious and a bit foolish if it's a move on your own team-mate.

"So Charles is kind of forcing, albeit not deliberately, Ferrari to make these decisions. He did race Lewis hard in Mexico City, and we saw what happened there, and he raced Lewis hard in Monza, and we saw what happened there."

Long regarded as one of the fastest drivers in the sport, Leclerc, 29, is a graduate of Ferrari's academy and joined their race team in 2019 after a debut season of F1 at Sauber.

He outperformed four-time champion Sebastian Vettel and then Carlos Sainz across their respective seasons as team-mates and was comfortably ahead of Hamilton by over 80 points after the Briton joined from Mercedes last year.

But Leclerc has faced a resurgent force in Hamilton this year, with the 41-year-old holding a 17-point advantage over him in the championship with two races to go.

"Charles is a fine driver, don't get me wrong, but his pole-to-win conversion rate (27 to nine) is not enough," added Croft on Leclerc's Ferrari record so far.

"You can also argue that the team haven't given him the car to make that conversion rate better, but he does make mistakes, we've seen that.

"We've seen in the past when he's been leading a race and he's crashed out all by himself. He's not the finished article and I don't want to be too harsh on Charles because I think he's a truly wonderful human being, but he's no Lewis Hamilton when it comes to his record and his performances and his consistency over the years."

Vasseur said he would hold fresh discussions with his drivers this week.

But do those talks need to now go further in terms of setting out firmly what is and is not acceptable - and establishing consequences for any transgressions?

Chadwick said: "I think the biggest issue [to this point] is the conversations haven't been serious enough.

"I think a clear-the-air talk as in 'okay it's not your fault, it's not your fault' and 'okay this is how things are' versus, actually, what are the rules of engagement? What are the reprimands if you do take your team-mate out and are they severe enough that actually neither driver is going to dare put themselves in that position?

"Clearly not because when you look at the move Charles did. Okay I kind of agree a little bit it wasn't not on, but it's definitely not on on your team-mate. I think you can maybe risk a move like Lando did on Lewis and I think that's also actually where Charles was a bit unlucky [in that he] went for it and then he kind of sees the door closing a bit and then he backs out and then it's kind of worse because he's over the kerb and that's what caused him to hit him.

"If he had actually just really committed to it maybe it would have been a bit better but, either way, you just never do that on your team-mate and clearly he didn't see there being any risk as to making a move like that on his team-mate. In his mind in that moment, Lewis is the same as any other driver on that grid. it's not a car in the same team as you.

"So that definitely needs a lot of discussion behind the scenes."

Chadwick, though, believes it is possible to win world titles with two No 1 drivers.

"I think it can still work with two drivers of top calibre but there has to be clear rules of engagement," she added.

"That's what we were arguably critical of, but it worked for McLaren last year."

But given the repeat nature of the on-track clashes and flashpoints between Hamilton and Leclerc this season, Croft is unsure much will actually change despite the incident and another round of discussions.

"So what do Ferrari do?" pondered Croft.

"They either say 'Lewis is No 1 going forward' and 'sorry, Charles, you're not going to get involved with this and you're going to drive for your team-mate because we need a championship here'. Or they get a new team principal who can actually maybe have a better sway over the two drivers, because at the moment it looks like whatever Fred says it just gets ignored out on track. Or they can just carry on as they are doing.

"And if I was going to put whatever dollars you had left over from Vegas on this one, I'd probably say Ferrari are just going to carry on and do what they did this year next year as well because they've had every chance so far this year to actually address the situation and they've not addressed it right so far."

articles.summary: La neerlandesa Viaplay, canal oficial de Max, no viaja, así como SKy Alemania o Canal+, que harán la retransmisión desde sus estudios centrales
articles.body: Los equipos de F1 ya han ido aterrizando en Qatar desde el lunes sin novedades de ningún tipo. El escenario en Oriente Medio, especialmente en Qatar, Dubai y Abu Dhabi parece estar calmado respecto a meses atrás y no habrá problemas para que se celebren los dos GP finales de la temporada en Lusail primero, este fin de seman y luego en Yas Marina, para poner el broche a este largo año de F1 2026. Los que no estarán al completo serán los medios audiovisuales, pues algunas de las operadoras de TV que tiene los derechos han preferido no desplazarse a estas carreras y trabajar desde casa, sin periodistas y cámaras en el paddock. Lo harán usando los recursos de F1-TV o la señal internacional que ofrecen. Según se está comentando en diversas informaciones, son tres las que no viajan, especialmente Viaplay, que incluso patrocina personalmente a Max Verstappen, Sky Alemania y Canal + Francia. Aquí no se trata de una cuestión de miedos a que pase algo, sino que en muchos casos depende de las coberturas de los seguros y de si se hacen responsables en determinados casos, lo que hace que se tome una decisión o la contraria. Según ha podido saber MARCA, DAZN F1 España sí acudirá y lo hará con una cobertura similar a la del resto de la temporada, como ya lo estuvo recientemente DAZN MotoGP hace dos semanas en el GP de Qatar de Motociclismo, donde estuvo a punto de decidirse el campeonato de la categoría reina, que luego llegó hasta Portimao. En principio no debería haber ningún tipo de problema, pues la F1 ha recabado las garantías posibles por parte de los dos gobiernos involucrados. El deporte está siendo completamente respetado por Irán, como ha sucedido en el baloncesto (SuperCup Euroleague), el pádel (Hexagon Cup) y el ya citado GP de Qatar de MotoGP. Sin ir más lejos, El Partizan visita hoy el Coca Cola Arena de Dubai en la Euroliga de Baloncesto, una competición que se está desarrollando sin incidentes de ningún tipo desde septiembre. Eso sí, las autoridades de Qatar no lo fían todo a la improvisación. Según publica 'Motor Sport Magazine' el circuito de Lusail tiene un protocolo de emergencia ante la posibilidad de un ataque o un atentado. El documento, fechado el 4 de noviembre, contempla el uso de distintas instalaciones del circuito, como refugios para los pilotos, integrantes de los equipos y demás personal del paddock. El mismo protocolo se preparó para el GP de MotoGP que se disputó hace unas semanas, sin que fuera necesaria su utilización.

articles.title: Bagnaia no podrá despedirse en Valencia y entra Lecuona
articles.standfirst: Sigue sin recibir al apto tras su dramática caída en Qatar y no estará en la que iba a ser la última carrera con Ducati Corse en MotoGP
articles.summary: Sigue sin recibir al apto tras su dramática caída en Qatar y no estará en la que iba a ser la última carrera con Ducati Corse en MotoGP
articles.body: Pecco Bagnaia sigue arrastrando secuelas importantes de su dramática caída en el Sprint de Qatar hace dos semanas y será baja para la última prueba de 2026 en Cheste, donde no podrá despedirse como quería del equipo de su vida, Ducati Corse, con el que fue campeón de MotoGP en 2022 y 2023. Así lo ha confirmado Lenovo Ducati de forma oficial este martes, así como que Iker Lecuona será el encargado de sustituirle en la cita del GP de la Comunidad Valenciana. Bagnaia (de 30 años), tenía la ilusión de un cierre emotivo en el Ricardo Tormo, después de ocho temporadas unido a la marca de Borgo Panigale, encima de la moto, pero las fracturas de dos dedos en el pie derecho sufridas en Lusail no están consolidadas, por lo que no podrá ser el compañero de Marc Márquez en el fin de fiesta de la temporada. Pero hay otra consecuencia, como es que el italiano tampoco podrá subirse al prototipo de la Aprilia RS GP27, con el que tenía previsto probar por primera vez en los test que tendrán lugar el martes posterior a la carrera en Cheste, cuando además es uno de los pocos que no ha podido testar aón la 850cc. que entra en vigor en 2027 en la categoría reina. Hay que recordar que Pecco ha firmado con Aprilia por las cuatro próximas temporadas, equipo con el que quiere renacer y optar de nuevo al título Mundial de MotoGP después de dos temporadas muy complicada para él, coincidiendo con la llegada de Marc a su lado. Por su parte Iker Lecuona, actual subcampeón del Mundial de SBK (Superbike), será el encargado de suplir a Bagnaia como ya hizo en Portimao y como le tocó anteriormente a lo largo de la temporadas tras las respectivas lesiones de Álex Márquez y Fermín Aldeguer. Su capacidad de adaptación y sus destacables resultados cada vez que ha sido requerido, le han valido la confianza de Ducati para correr en casa ante su público, lo que es un bonito premio para él.

articles.title: Williams in minor breach of F1 cost cap for 2025 season and take financial and wind tunnel time penalties
articles.summary: Williams "unintentionally committed" spending and procedural breach of 2025 budget cap after overspending by £627,000; Alpine found in procedural breach; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
articles.body:
The FIA announced Williams had accepted an Accepted Breach Agreement after being found to have "unintentionally committed" a minor overspend and procedural breach of the sport's spending rules for last year.

Williams overspent by £627,000 - 0.48 per cent over the 2025 cost cap - and in addition to a financial penalty, will receive a 1.5 per cent reduction in wind tunnel and CFD testing time over the next 12 months. The 2025 spending cap was $135m (£102m) plus inflation.

An FIA statement read: "The Cost Cap Administration recognised that WGPE [Williams Grand Prix Engineering Limited] has acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process, provided additional information and evidence in a timely manner when so requested and that there is no evidence that WGPE has sought or obtained any advantage [sporting or otherwise] as a result of the identified breaches."

Explaining the nature of the breach, Williams, who finished fifth in last year's Constructors' Championship but are ninth with two races of this year to go, said in a statement: "The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure. We believed these costs fell outside of the cap." A minor breach is defined as an overspend of less than five per cent of the cost cap.

"Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

"The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

"Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future. We have always been and will continue to be strong supporters of the cost cap, which naturally requires accurate policing to be effective."

Alpine were found to have committed a procedural breach, related to inaccuracies in their full year reporting documentation.

The FIA noted that they had also "acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process and has sought to provide additional information and evidence when requested in a timely manner and that there is no accusation or evidence that Alpine has sought or obtained any undue advantage". Alpine's spending was below the cost cap limit.

Alpine will pay a financial penalty to the FIA after also entering into an accepted breach agreement for the procedural breach.

All nine other teams, which included 2026 newcomers Cadillac, were found to be in compliance for 2025, along with all five power unit manufacturers for their respective spending cap.

articles.title: Newbury's Coral Gold Cup: Jamie Lynch's horse-by-horse guide to Saturday's feature handicap chase live on Sky Sports Racing
articles.summary: Ahead of the big Coral Gold Cup showdown on Saturday, Sky Sports Racing's senior form analyst Jamie Lynch offers his verdict on every runner going to post in search of top honours; watch the race at 3pm on Saturday - LIVE on Sky Sports Racing
articles.body:
The Coral Gold Cup at Newbury at 3pm is one of the biggest and best handicap chases of the entire season, although conditions will be a break from the norm - the reason the race is a little lighter at the top end this time, with only one rated above 150.

But there is the usual stack of classy second-season chasers with high trajectories and higher aspirations, meaning that - as always - it's going to take a lot of winning. Let's look at all those entered for this high-prestige prize, just one part of a stellar Saturday on Sky Sports Racing.

Watch every race of the Coral Gold Cup meeting from Newbury live on Sky Sports Racing on Friday 27th and Saturday 28th November.

He ran the race of his life when beating all bar Panic Attack in last year's renewal, conceding weight all round, the same again here, but he hasn't reproduced that level since, though one race was the Grand National and the latest smacked of a prep run, off a break and ridden by a 7lb conditional jockey.

The last top-weight winner was the daddy, Denman, whose mark was 20lb higher, if you don't mind.

Has had the privilege of residing at two of the finest horseracing hotels in history, trained firstly by Nicky Henderson and then Willie Mullins, for whom he won the Galway Plate in July against the odds, as the outsider of the stable's four.

That has left him with what's probably too high a mark now, so says the Kerry National in which he finished an unthreatening sixth.

A nephew of the legendary Denman, who had a mark of 161 when he made a successful reappearance in this race in his second season over fences, Regent's Stroll is not quite on the same trajectory but ended his novice campaign on a high at the Festivals. He was third at Cheltenham to Meetmebythesea and Gold Dancer in the Jack Richards and second to the latter in the Mildmay.

We haven't seen all he's got, including for stamina, and the stable can still get one primed and readied for this, highlighted by Kandoo Kid in 2024. Big chance.

He was third in the Kerry National last time where his status as favourite spoke of his developing talent, having caught the eye in the Plates at both Cheltenham and Galway. Being a second-season chaser from the Henry de Bromhead yard is reason enough to put him on a shortlist, and then there are the added bonuses of his untapped stamina and suitability to non-November ground.

The classic profile for this race, as a second-season chaser with a touch of class and an eye on the biggest staying prizes: the most memorable winners of the Hennessy, now the Coral Gold Cup, have all had a look of Wendigo. He was rated 147 following his third to Kitzbuhel in the Kauto Star almost a year ago, and he's still rated that now, perhaps generously so.

The signs from his reappearance were loud and clear that he's an improved model, to give 10lb to Potters Charm and a heavy beating to Doyen Quest at Carlisle, all without the need to play his ace card, the stamina card. If you tasked AI with creating a Coral Gold Cup winner, the technical drawings would be of Wendigo.

This horse missed the whole of last season, not that anybody could have told from his finding, grinding comeback win - at odds of 33/1 - in a 16-runner handicap hurdle at Newbury, like he'd never been away.

As a novice chaser, he was second to The Jukebox Man in the Grade Two John Francome in 2024, as well as third to Jagwar in the Plate at the Cheltenham Festival. That form makes a mark of 147 well within reach, though the 'bounce' factor is obviously high with him.

The heroine of last year, but she was coming in hot then, unlike now, absent since April. Also, she's 6lb higher now, or effectively 9lb considering that Tristan Durrell claimed 3lb back then.

History tells us how hard a repeat is - Arkle being the only one to ever do it in back-to-back years.

Stuart Edmunds' charge was classy but clumsy as a novice chaser, exemplified by the Mildmay at Aintree, where he went off 7/2 and looked a threat when he came down at the fourth-last. Only Masaccio prevented the perfect prep in a hurdle at Newbury, and Miami Magic has got the game to win a race like this.

He's unbothered by drying ground, but there are 21 fences and almost as many rivals in his way, an unforgiving environment for a sketchy jumper.

A magical metamorphosis through last season, which started with a PU and a UR and ended in two 'wow' wins, culminating with the National Hunt Chase.

A 10lb hit requires her to pick up where she left off and then some, and the unseasonable autumn has impeded her traditional stable more than most, raising some doubt as to whether she'll be razor sharp first time out.

The small print reads differently to Regent's Stroll and Wendigo but the formula fabric is still the same, as a second-season chaser from a leading yard. His reappearance over hurdles was a means to an end, not much in the way of bite even so, after a summer wind op, and this track is very different to right-handed Ascot where he's looked most at home as a chaser.

Trainers: Lucinda Russell and Michael Scudamore

This contender fell when favourite for this 12 months ago, the omen for a season which was essentially a write-off. But, with the reset button pressed over the summer, he was back looking more the Myretown of old in dismissing a trio of inferior rivals at Kelso, a confidence-restoring exercise, as well as a greater connecting point back to his showstopper in the 2025 Ultima. That was the reason he topped the market last year off the same mark as now.

Got better as a novice and showed he can cut it in big-field handicaps with his placings in the Kim Muir and the bet365 Gold Cup, beaten a neck in one and a neck and a short-head in the other. Won a mere maiden chase on his return at Galway but was as big as 9/2 that day, on account of the trip (an inadequate 2m 2f), putting him ahead of schedule for his primary target, at a track that plugs into his properties.

In his time with Henry de Bromhead, he was 0/6 with his British raids, including pulling up in the latest Grand National at 100/1, and his first start for Chris Gordon amounted to little, albeit over hurdles and without the usual tongue tie.

Seems a lot older than seven, largely because he's high mileage (began with Sir Michael Stoute), which made his spring surge all the more remarkable, not returning until January but improving 25lb and bringing up the hat-trick in the bet365 Gold Cup. As a late bloomer with a come-from-behind style, his ceiling isn't so discernible as many in here.

The chief sufferer in the chaotic start when 14/1 for this last year (trained by Alan King), which was more of a window of opportunity for him than this renewal, having lost a bit of lustre in the meantime, for all that his first start for Nick Scholfield when runner-up at Market Rasen suggested that most of his ability was intact.

Two for two in handicap chases at Newbury, the first all down to Sean Bowen (having traded at 880/1 in-running) and the second coming on his reappearance on this very day last year, in the 2m 6f event. The rest of the campaign was a bit of a washout but who knows what he can do at this sort of trip, back fresh and back at Newbury? He's something of a mystery box.

Thrived in big fields as a hurdler, and his first experience of such a scenario as a chaser prompted a fine third in the National Hunt Chase, after which he was excusably overwhelmed in the Irish National. Another to use the staying hurdle here earlier in the month as a stepping stone to this, and his component parts qualify him as a lively longshot, in the same way his dam's half-brother Madison Du Berlais was when he won this at 25/1 in 2008.

Some going and some stamina to win the Scottish National as a novice, on ground that was officially heavy. But he's not one dimensional, nor maxed out, based on an encouraging return at Aintree, and he's only a six-year-old. A field, or a jumping test, such as this holds no fears for him.

His success in a high-value handicap at Aintree on National day is the one and only time he's tackled 3m+ over fences, no coincidence in that, nor the fact he has saved his second go for this, after a screw-tightening reappearance over 2m 4f at Stratford. This perceptible plan, and the man orchestrating it (Dan Skelton), are big selling points.

This contender started with a bang for Skelton at Cheltenham and perhaps had a hangover from that when underwhelming at Aintree a fortnight later. He's in a similar boat but not the same mould as Panic Attack from last year.

The likes of Wendigo and Regent's Stroll speak for themselves, both a profiler's dream for this race, but, for that very reason, the market is giving nothing away for either. The ill-fated Gold Dancer beat both in the Mildmay, and his form is tied in with DOWNMEXICOWAY , who has got in some valuable practice for big-field handicaps while continually hinting at better to come.

articles.title: Formula 1: Williams exceeded cost cap by £627,000
articles.summary: Williams "unintentially" broke Formula 1's cost cap during the 2025 season, governing body the FIA finds.
articles.body:
Williams broke Formula 1's cost cap during the 2025 season, governing body the FIA has found.

The team say they "unintentionally" exceeded the cap by £627,000. Last season, the spending limit was $135m (£106m).

Alpine were also found to have broken the rules, although theirs was a procedural breach without overspending.

Both teams have reached so-called 'accepted breach agreements' with the FIA.

Williams' involves a financial penalty, the amount of which has not been disclosed, and a 1.5% reduction in permitted aerodynamic research and development time for the next 12 months.

Alpine have also been given an undisclosed financial penalty.

Both teams must foot the costs of the investigations by the FIA into their rule-breaking.

A Williams statement said: "The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure.

"We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

"The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted co-operatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

"Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future."

The FIA said in a statement: "There is no accusation or evidence that (Williams) sought at any time to act in bad faith, dishonestly or in a fraudulent manner, nor that it wilfully concealed any information from the cost-cap administration.

"The financial regulations are complex, and the breaches arose from an interpretation adopted by (Williams) in good faith.

"Williams has accepted the FIA's interpretation and the resulting breaches."

It said Williams' breach was the equivalent of a 0.48% overspend, which "falls at the lower end of the less than 5% minor overspend range".

Williams' costs were incurred as the team tried to update their operations in order to become more competitive.

Williams had targeted the new 2026 regulations as an opportunity to make a significant step forwards in the team's attempt to return to the front of F1.

Instead, the team have taken a step backwards, and after finishing fifth in 2025, are lying ninth in the constructors' championship with two races remaining this season.

Alpine said in a statement: "The team accepts that it unknowingly committed a procedural breach, which is a result of inaccuracies in the full-year reporting documentation for costs related to exclusions and adjustments.

"The errors and inaccuracies in the reporting were specifically related to non-sporting and operational costs which the CCA recognised didn't give the team any performance advantage, such as marketing activities, non-F1 activities, HR activities, employees' bonus costs, offsetting of costs, and costs of inventories."

articles.title: ¡Williams es sancionado por pasarse del presupuesto en 2025!
articles.standfirst: La FIA publica la revisión del límite del año pasado y los de Grove serán sancionados... después de un año y un coche para olvidar
articles.summary: La FIA publica la revisión del límite del año pasado y los de Grove serán sancionados... después de un año y un coche para olvidar
articles.body: Si Williams F1 no había tenido suficiente con un año funesto y horrible en lo deportivo, con el coche más pesado y peor evolucionado en 2026, ahora le llega la puntilla, con una resolución de la FIA que prevé consecuencias en forma de multa y de penalización, que supondrá de reducción de horas en el túnel de viento, por nada menos que los próximos 12 meses. Es el colofón a una gestión por parte de James Vowles y su equipo directivo que queda en entredicho de una forma evidente, pues en 2025 no incorporaron ni una sola pieza para evolucionar el FW-47 en toda la temporada, a pesar de lo cual Carlos Sainz logró dos podios. se intentaban centrar en el nuevo reglamento... y el coche de este año el FW-48, que no ha podido más decepcionante. No sólo no llegaron a los primeros test en Barcelona, sino que luego se revelaron como un monocasco que se pasaba 28 kilos del peso mínimo, ya que hubo de ser reforzado para pasar los crash test en el invierno, lo que lastró todo su rendimiento y toda su evolución... El chasis aligerado no llegó hasta Bakú, pasada la mitad de la temporada, pero eso no cambió la nula eficiencia en todo tipo de curvas del actual monoplaza de Sainz. La FIA ha completado la revisión del límite presupuestario de 2025 y ha comunicado de forma oficial que Williams excedió el máximo en aproximadamente 750.000 euros (un 0,48%) sobre lo permitido para todos. Los de Vowles y la Federación Internacional han llegado a un acuerdo (ABA), que tendrá una penalización con multa económica, además de algo peor. Tendrán una reducción del 1,5% en las pruebas en túnel de viento y CFD (dinámica computacional de fluidos) durante los próximos 12 meses, lo que va afectar sin duda al coche de 2027 y a su posterior desarrollo. Para Red Bull o Mercedes sería inapreciable, pero para los de Grove, con el déficit de eficiencia y rendimiento que arrastran ahora puede ser grave. La pregunta es ¿en qué se gastaron el dinero con tan pobres resultados?. Williams intenta explicarlo en un comunicado. "La infracción se refiere a los gastos administrativos en los que incurrimos al realizar cambios en la estructura de nuestra empresa. Creíamos que estos gastos quedaban fuera del límite. Tras las conversaciones con la FIA, hemos acordado resolver el asunto de acuerdo con su interpretación de que dichos gastos deberían haber estado incluidos en el límite", argumentan Williams también ha infringido el procedimiento, algo que también le ha sucedido a Alpine, con lo que los de Enstone ha aceptado la multa prevista.

articles.title: Max Verstappen admits he would “rather stay at home” ahead of Qatar and Abu Dhabi
articles.summary: Speaking to Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf, Max Verstappen made no secret of his discomfort ahead of Formula 1’s Middle East double-header
articles.body:
Formula 1's paddock is touching down in Doha for the penultimate round of the 2026 championship, yet Max Verstappen is not pretending the trip sits easily with him.

Speaking to Dutch outlet De Telegraaf , the four-time world champion delivered a blunt assessment of finishing the 23-race calendar in Qatar and Abu Dhabi amid ongoing regional hostilities.

"Do I feel comfortable with it? No, I'd rather stay at home," Verstappen said. "But we've been given certain guarantees, and therefore we have to assume they're true. It's not exactly pleasant to go somewhere knowing that rockets can still fly over your head in the surrounding countries. But, anyway, we're going."

F1 cancelled April's Saudi Arabian Grand Prix outright and relocated the Bahrain round to Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit in October - a race Verstappen went on to win from pole - due to the conflict in the Middle East. For months, officials kept Italy's Imola circuit on standby as a cold-weather contingency for the finale, only to stand down those backup plans on 10 November once all 11 teams backed completing the calendar in the Gulf.

Writing on Instagram the same day, FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem declared the governing body ready for both venues.

"We are fully prepared and committed to delivering two outstanding grand prix weekends and a spectacular conclusion to the [F1 championship]," Ben Sulayem wrote, adding that officials are "working closely with our partners to ensure everything is in place for our drivers, teams and fans".

Inside the paddock, drivers have struck noticeably different tones over the past month. Ahead of October's United States Grand Prix, Grand Prix Drivers' Association director Carlos Sainz openly questioned the championship's certainty, telling reporters: "They seem very convinced that it's going to go ahead. On my personal side, I'm not," while urging everyone to "stay diligent, and reactive to whatever happens".

By contrast, fellow GPDA director George Russell told British media in Las Vegas that he has "no hesitation" in travelling to Qatar and the United Arab Emirates despite official travel warnings, while McLaren 's Lando Norris said he trusts F1 bosses would not place the championship's roughly 2,000 travelling staff in harm's way.

Once cars roll out for Friday practice at the Losail International Circuit (27-29 November) before the season closes in Abu Dhabi (4-6 December), Verstappen still has plenty to protect.

Although 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli wrapped up the drivers' title in Mexico City and Mercedes sealed its ninth constructors' crown in Sao Paulo, Red Bull's late-season turnaround has put Verstappen on a nine-race podium streak - including four victories in his last six outings.

Fresh off winning Las Vegas's 352-overtake thriller, Verstappen sits second in the standings on 304 points, holding a 37-point advantage over Lewis Hamilton (267) and 40 over Russell and Norris (264 apiece) with 50 driver points remaining. Crucially, Red Bull's 440–431 edge over McLaren for third in the constructors' standings - worth millions in prize payouts - remains razor-thin with 86 team points still on the board.

Qatar itself drops its sprint format for 2026, yet Pirelli and the FIA added a fresh strategic wrinkle on Wednesday by mandating a 27-lap maximum stint length per tyre set across Sunday's 57-lap Grand Prix - guaranteeing a minimum two-stop contest. Verstappen may have preferred spending late November elsewhere, but with Red Bull's constructors' finish still on the line, he will have little time to look anywhere except the road ahead.

articles.title: Analysts side with Hamilton after Las Vegas: 'That felt too harsh'
articles.summary: Former Formula 1 drivers Jolyon Palmer and David Coulthard both believe the time penalty Lewis Hamilton received was too harsh at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. O...
articles.body:
Former Formula 1 drivers Jolyon Palmer and David Coulthard both believe the time penalty Lewis Hamilton received was too harsh at the Las Vegas Grand Prix .

On Saturday evening in Las Vegas, Hamilton received a 10-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage when overtaking Lando Norris.

The Briton was not satisfied with the stewards' call over the team radio. "That's bulls***t! If I'd turned in, we'd have crashed. Isn't that interesting? One race where someone is given mitigating circumstances, they give them five seconds and then they give me 10 seconds for avoiding an incident."

Palmer compared the incident to what happened at the Mexico City Grand Prix, where Charles Leclerc cut the corner on the opening lap to stay in first place. For that incident, the Monegasque driver received only a five-second time penalty.

"Leclerc did a similar thing on Hamilton, got a 5-second penalty which was deemed to be not really harsh enough for a lead change at that point," Palmer said during the broadcast," the Briton said on F1 TV's broadcast.

Coulthard continued: "Yeah, this feels too harsh for the scenario and what makes it tricky is Leclerc got past Norris and, therefore, when Lewis is looking in his mirrors, he's gone, 'Okay, well I may have passed him off track, but he's now a person behind me.'"

Palmer then concluded: "It's exactly what happened in Mexico"

In their verdict, the stewards' wrote: "Car 1 (NOR) attempted to overtake Car 44 (HAM) on the left-hand side approaching Turn 7. At the apex, the front axle of Car 1 was at least alongside of the mirror of Car 44. Applying the Driving Standards Guidelines, the Stewards determined that Car 1 was entitled to the corner.

"Car 44 remained alongside Car 1 and subsequently crossed the white line on the right-hand side, leaving the track. By doing so, Car 44 avoided a potential collision but maintained its position ahead of Car 1.

"By leaving the track while defending, Car 44 therefore is considered as having gained a lasting advantage. Car 44 did not concede the position to Car 1, as he should have done. The Stewards therefore determined that Car 44 had left the track and gained a lasting advantage."

articles.standfirst: Renueva sus expectativas para el año próximo y ese sigue siendo el principal motivo para seguir
articles.summary: Renueva sus expectativas para el año próximo y ese sigue siendo el principal motivo para seguir
articles.body: Fernando Alonso habla claro sobre la situación actual de sus coche y del motor Honda, pero renueva sus expectativas para 2027, tras un curso plagado de contratiempos y de premura en el desarrollo de ambos grandes elementos, la aerodinámica, que enderezaron a mitad de año, y la mecánica, que espera que se mejore para la próxima temporada. "A nivel de motor, estamos muy lejos y no podemos ser competitivos con la unidad de potencia que tenemos. Hay circuitos como Las Vegas en los que perdemos más de dos segundos por vuelta solo en las rectas, y la fiabilidad tampoco está al nivel que debería estar. Nadie está contento con cómo van las cosas en lo que respecta a la unidad de potencia, pero sabemos que Honda está trabajando duro para mejorar la situación", ha afirmado en una entrevista en la web oficial de Aston Martin F1. "La actualización del chasis de Budapest debía aportar una determinada ganancia en tiempo por vuelta, y la aportó. Fuimos competitivos en Budapest y conseguimos puntos en Zandvoort y Malasia", recuerda Alonso, sobre algo que se cuantificó en su día entre 1,5 segundos y 2, en un solo salto. Con otro motor, la histori hubiera sido muy distinta. "Hemos conseguido meternos en el grupo de la zona media con una sola gran actualización del chasis esta temporada así que eso me ha dado la confianza de que sabemos en qué dirección vamos y la convicción de que solo es cuestión de tiempo que tengamos un muy buen coche". "Después de los test de pretemporada en Bahrein y de la primera carrera en Australia, todo el mundo entendió dónde estábamos. Nadie se escondió de la realidad y, desde el primer momento, nos centramos en cómo solucionar cada uno de los problemas. Ver el trabajo y el compromiso que hay entre bambalinas me da confianza de cara al próximo año", asegura un Fernando que si ha decidido seguir es porque cree que el AMR27 supondrá un claro ascenso respecto al anterior. Hay que recordar que el plan de Honda, que ya fue desvelado hace un mes, tendrá dos escalones en 2027. Un primero que llegará desde los test de pretemporada y hasta el primer tercio del año, donde esperan superar los grandes problemas de la unidad actual, con un rediseño global de la parte de la combustión, el ERS y las baterías. Y un segundo que podría estar en torno a la llegada a Europa, posiblemente Portimao, donde se quiere dar el salto en prestaciones definitivo para equipararse a la mayoría de unidades de la parrilla.

articles.title: Qatar GP: Explaining 2026 tyre-limit rule and what impact it will have on F1 race weekend at Lusail International Circuit
articles.summary: Why a lap limit on tyre usage is again in place at Lusail as we explain, with the help of Bernie Collins, what impact it might have on the weekend; watch every session from the Qatar GP live Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
articles.body:
Qatar stages the first of those, with the fast, flowing Lusail International Circuit hosting a Grand Prix for the fifth occasion since its debut in 2021.

As was the case last year, a tyre limit regulation is in place for the race, so what is it and what impact might it have on the weekend?

What's the Qatar Grand Prix tyre rule for 2026?

Pirelli, Formula 1's tyre supplier, last week announced there will be a limit of 27 laps on a set of tyres for this weekend in Qatar.

It is the third time a tyre limit has been implemented for the race at the Lusail International Circuit after punctures at the inaugural 2021 event, and safety concerns being raised during the 2023 weekend.

In 2023, Pirelli mandated a three-stop race and last year they implemented a 25-lap limit which effectively created a two-stop race.

The Qatar Grand Prix is 57 laps so the 27-lap limit for this weekend means, like last year, each driver will need to pit at least twice.

Pirelli explained "the increase [in the limit] has been made possible by the lower load levels recorded so far on the current generation of cars and by a further reinforcement of the tyre construction".

Laps to the grid, formation laps and laps after the chequered flag do not count towards the lap total but laps will be counted cumulatively across all track sessions.

In effect, that means if a driver does three laps on a set of tyres in qualifying, and uses those tyres in the race, they can only do another 24 laps on them before changing in the Grand Prix.

"This precautionary measure is linked to the unique characteristics of the Lusail circuit, which is particularly demanding in terms of energy loads, thermal stress and tread wear," added Pirelli.

What will the impact of the rule be on the Qatar race weekend?

Sky Sports F1's Bernie Collins, a former head of race strategy at Aston Martin, answers several of the key questions around the rule…

Bernie: "Qatar is a very high-speed track and there used to be some very aggressive, sharp-edged kerbs that led to some cuts in the sidewalls of tyres.

"That resulted in quite strong limits on the number of laps in 2023 when an 18-lap tyre limit was imposed.

"That very short limit combined with very hot conditions that year, when the race was held in October, made it very difficult for drivers. They were pushing very hard every lap in very high temperatures, which is one of the reasons why we now declare a heat hazard if it's over 31 degrees and drivers can wear a cooling vest.

"Since then, the track has removed some of the harshest edges of the kerbs, which resulted, alongside some cool conditions, teams attempting a one-stop strategy in the 2024 race.

"The difficulty with that was that even though the tyres were now not getting damaged, there was still lots of wear on the tyre because of the high-speed nature of the track. The tyre was wearing down on the surface more than Pirelli were happy with on those one-stop strategies which is why last year we had a 25-lap limit imposed and this year we have 27-lap limit."

How will it change how the teams prepare?

Bernie: "I think teams will have a heads up from Pirelli way before we found out, so they'll have had much longer to prepare for it.

"I think because it's not a Sprint weekend, teams have quite a good allocation of medium or hard tyres in order to do what they need to do. The problem with a Sprint weekend, which Qatar was last year, is that the 25-lap limit also applied through the Sprint itself and Qualifying as it's all cumulative through the weekend.

"So this year, with a normal weekend, and particularly with the medium tyres, the teams have loads available to play with.

"So I'd expect the race to be similar to last year in terms of something like two sets of medium and one set of hard. They will probably still run a hard tyre in Practice Two to try it and then they'll save one for their race allocation. Some teams might save two for the race allocation.

"But I think with it not being a Sprint, the teams should have loads of tyres available to make it happen and it'll just depend on whether they think medium or hard is their preferred tyre for the race."

Bernie: "I don't think the 27-lap limit is very restrictive in terms of strategy because there is lots of freedom with the 57-lap race.

"The earliest you could stop and still do a two-stop race is lap three. So you'd do three laps on one tyre and then one stint of 27 laps followed by another of 27 laps. That strategy might be possible if there's a Safety Car early in the race, meaning you'd have to do one more stop to the end.

"We're not expecting really hot conditions, but not really cold conditions either, so I think the 27-lap limit, depending on when you stop, won't necessarily mean that the drivers can push every single lap. It won't be tyre management and more tyre management because drivers are doing a one-stop, but it won't be pushing every single lap with really short stints like we had in 2023 with the 18-lap limit either. It will be somewhere in between."

Could the rule advantage or disadvantage anyone?

Bernie: "It's hard to say which teams might benefit, or who the rule might hurt, because unlike previous years, we've not had teams really suffering more than others with tyre degradation.

"So I think it's not necessarily going to benefit a lot of teams."

Will teams be wary of avoiding McLaren's 2025 mistake of not pitting under an early Safety Car?

Bernie: "In 2025, the Safety Car came out on lap seven, which was exactly the right lap that you could make it to the end by doing one more stop. McLaren were the only team not to take that and suffered, losing positions as a result.

"This year the lap that can happen is lap three.

"That is very early in the race but because the pit loss in Qatar is so long (26.5s) if the degradation is low enough, which will be driven by track temperature, then you should take the Safety Car stop early on and try to do one stop from there because the saving under the Safety Car is significant compared to the time lost with the pit stop."
